level-1.title: Sorting needs from wants
summary: Some things are needs for one person and wants for another.
A bus pass is a need if you must travel to school.
The same item can be both. School shoes are a need. A tenth pair is a want.
Ask two questions. What happens if I do not buy this? Can I wait?
Advertisements try to make wants feel like needs.

questions.prompt: You already own a working umbrella. A shop advertises a 'must-have' new umbrella. Using the two questions from the lesson, what should you ask first?

image.alt: An advertisement for an umbrella beside an old working umbrella

options.label: What happens if I don't buy this, and can I wait?
Will my friends like the new umbrella?
How much does the shop want me to spend?

questions.hint: The lesson gives you exactly two questions to ask before any purchase.

questions.prompt: You live 10 minutes' walk from school, but a friend has a bicycle you could buy to get there faster. Applying the two questions, is the bicycle a need?

image.alt: A short walking path to school beside a bicycle

options.label: Yes - anything that helps you get to school is a need
No - you can already reach school on foot, so it fails 'what happens if I don't buy it'

questions.hint: Ask what happens if you do NOT buy it. Can you still get to school?

questions.prompt: An advertisement says 'Buy these shoes now, offer ends today!' and you already have shoes that fit well. What is really happening?

image.alt: A bright advertisement board with a countdown

options.label: It genuinely is a need because the offer will end
The ad is using urgency to turn a want into a fake emergency
You must decide within the hour

questions.hint: A real need does not depend on a shop's clock.

level-2.title: Needs, wants and spending priorities
summary: Adults sort spending into fixed costs and flexible costs.
Rent and school fees are fixed. They stay the same each month.
Snacks and outings are flexible. You control them.
When money is short, cut flexible costs first.
The 24 hour rule helps. Wait one day before buying a want over ₹500.

questions.prompt: Rent is ₹5000 a month. This month you only have ₹4700 left after all your flexible spending. What went wrong?

image.alt: A house with a rent bill and an empty wallet

options.label: Rent should be paid late instead
Flexible spending should have been cut before it ate into money needed for the fixed rent
Nothing went wrong, this is normal

questions.hint: Fixed costs like rent cannot shrink. Flexible costs can - and should, before it's too late.

questions.prompt: Money is short this month. Which of these should you cut FIRST: school fees, weekend outings, or medicine?

image.alt: An almost empty wallet beside school fees, outings, and medicine

options.label: Weekend outings - the only flexible one of the three
School fees, because they are the biggest
Medicine, because it is optional

questions.hint: Only one of the three can safely shrink without hurting you.

questions.prompt: You see a ₹450 want and a ₹600 want on the same day. To which one does the 24 hour rule apply?

image.alt: Two price tags, one below and one above five hundred rupees

options.label: Only the ₹600 one - the rule is for wants over ₹500
Neither, the rule is only for needs
Both, the rule applies to every purchase

questions.hint: Check the rule's exact price cutoff from the lesson.

level-3.title: How sellers get you to spend
summary: Sellers study how people decide, and design offers to make you buy more.
An "original price" crossed out makes a discount look bigger. Compare the price with other shops, not with the crossed-out number.
"Buy now, pay later" and small EMIs make a big price feel small. Add up every payment to see the real cost.
Subscriptions take a little every month and are easy to forget. Twelve small payments add up to one large one.
Cost per use is a smarter test. A ₹1,000 pair of shoes worn 200 times costs ₹5 per use.
Seeing friends buy something makes it feel like a need. Ask whether you would still want it if nobody else had it.

questions.prompt: Phone A costs ₹12,000 in one payment. Phone B is "only ₹1,100 a month" for 12 months. Which costs more in total?

image.alt: Two phones, one with a single price and one with a monthly price

options.label: Phone A, because ₹12,000 is a bigger number
Phone B, because 12 × ₹1,100 is ₹13,200
They cost exactly the same

questions.hint: Multiply the monthly payment by the number of months.

questions.prompt: You pay for a ₹150-a-month music app, a ₹99-a-month game pass and a ₹199-a-month video app. How much do they cost in one year?

image.alt: Three small monthly charges on a calendar

questions.hint: Add the three monthly amounts, then multiply by 12.

questions.prompt: Shoes X cost ₹600 and last 50 wears. Shoes Y cost ₹1,500 and last 300 wears. Which is cheaper per use?

image.alt: Two pairs of shoes with their prices

options.label: Shoes Y, at ₹5 a wear against ₹12
Shoes X, because ₹600 is less than ₹1,500
Both cost the same per wear

questions.hint: Divide each price by how many times you can use it.
